note: Confirmed detection misses found by reading target source by hand, not by the scanner. Each row names the sink, the caller-controlled input path, and the reason the current rule could not see it. `inScope` means the rule that owns the pattern exists and should have caught it; `outOfScope` means no rule covers the pattern at all. Proofs under `proof/` are re-implementations of the target's own string building, run locally; the target servers were still never executed.
reviewer: AI-assisted source review plus automated triage (see methodology.md); no independent human second pass

sink.code: return any(path.startswith(d) for d in self.__allowed_paths)

steps: the MCP tool argument `path` is a plain str validated by `validate_path` (pydantic AfterValidator)
src/core/validations.py:35 normalises with os.path.abspath
src/core/validations.py:48 hands the absolute path to __validate_absolute_path
src/core/validations.py:27 calls ServerConfig().is_allowed_path
src/core/config.py:17 does a bare str.startswith against each allowlist entry

missed.why: No separator is appended, so the check is a string prefix and not a path containment. With an allowlist of /home/user/safe, the requested path /home/user/safe-evil/secret.txt passes and is read.
missed.whyScannerMissed: traversal.js only fires on a join *expression* (path.join / Path /). Here the join happens earlier via os.path.abspath, the result is stored in a local, and the comparison happens in a different module. The guard-clamp machinery is keyed to the sink expression and never sees a startswith() that takes an already-resolved absolute path.

proof.observed: 0 path-traversal findings; the only finding is weak-allowlist (high, 'no metacharacter check')

missed.proposedChange: When a local is assigned from an absolute-path normaliser (abspath / resolve / realpath) and its containing function ends in an allowlist prefix test, treat the pair as a traversal sink and grade the comparison for separator awareness. Requires the same variable-aware association that 0.4.0 started in gated(); this is its cross-function form.
missed.expectedImprovement: Finds the class of 'resolved then prefix-tested' bugs, which is the most common shape in Python filesystem servers here (2 of 14 targets).
missed.regressionTest: benchmark/cases/path/bypass-resolved-prefix: helper returning os.path.abspath, caller testing startswith(ALLOWED) without sep, expect one high path-traversal.

steps: caller `pattern` reaches index.ts:594, only `"` is escaped

index.ts:271 joins the pipeline with ` | ` and again escapes only `"`

missed.why: Double quotes inside a double-quoted sh -c string do not stop `$( )` or backticks. pattern = "$(id)" reaches the shell unsubstituted. The path partner is escaped correctly (idx 289 escapes $ and backtick) but the pattern is not, which also makes the asymmetry visible inside one file.
missed.whyScannerMissed: shell-injection is JS/TS-only and only looks for caller values passed as the *first argument* to exec/execSync. Here the first argument is a template literal built three functions away from the sink, so CALLER_ARG sees `${joined}` rather than a caller-derived local. shell-exec fires but has no severity escalation and settles on 'pattern match only'.

missed.proposedChange: Follow a template literal to the locals it interpolates (one hop) before deciding the argument is not caller-controlled, and treat execAsync/exec with a template-literal argument as a shell sink in the same way as a bare variable.
missed.expectedImprovement: Removes the largest single source of 'inconclusive' in the TS sample and turns a real critical into a critical.
missed.regressionTest: benchmark/cases/shell/via-template: const cmd = `grep -i "${pattern}"`; execAsync(cmd), expect critical shell-injection.

steps: tool argument cmd and args are both plain strings
line 31-33 packs them into a two-element list
line 36 splats the list into create_subprocess_exec (no shell)

missed.why: The server's entire purpose is running an arbitrary program. There is no shell, so command injection is off the table, but the executable and its argument string are caller-chosen - that is arbitrary code execution by design. A tool that hands the model a shell and reports itself clean is the worst possible grade for a reader.
missed.whyScannerMissed: create_subprocess_exec and create_subprocess_shell appear in no rule. capability.js lists execSync|exec|spawn|execFile|subprocess.run|os.system|sh -c|bash -c; asyncio.create_subprocess_* is absent from capability.js, shell-input.js and every other rule.

proof.method: Direct read of server.py:29-40 and the tool schema at 81-98; both inputs are declared strings with no enum and no allowlist.
proof.observed: logical consequence of create_subprocess_exec with caller argv - no shell parsing, so the risk is executable/argument choice rather than metacharacters

missed.proposedChange: Add asyncio.create_subprocess_exec and create_subprocess_shell to the capability sink list, and emit two different findings: shell-exec when the argv is caller-derived (executable choice), shell-injection only for create_subprocess_shell. Do not reuse shell-injection's severity for exec.
missed.expectedImprovement: Two whole targets stop grading A while executing arbitrary commands (this repo and any other aiohttp/asyncio server).
missed.regressionTest: benchmark/cases/exec/aio-subprocess-exec (caller argv, expect high shell-exec) and .../aio-subprocess-shell (string command, expect critical shell-injection).
